messages.content: Survey recent Lyman-alpha forest constraints on warm dark matter. How do they compare with sterile-neutrino non-resonant production? Use the sterile-nu tools for production fractions.

**Survey** — 39 tools on 3 servers, 6 read-only probes, 11 papers found.

High-redshift Lyman-alpha forest flux power spectra are among the strongest constraints on the free-streaming of warm dark matter (WDM). The 95% CL lower limits on the thermal-relic mass have tightened over time: about 0.75 keV (Narayanan et al. 2000), 3.3 keV (Viel et al. 2013, HIRES/MIKE, z>4), 3.1 keV (Villasenor et al. 2022, 1080 Cholla simulations on Boera et al. 2019 data, with a weak likelihood peak near 4.5 keV) and 5.7 keV (Irsic et al. 2023, HIRES/UVES at z=4.2-5.0 with k_max=0.2 s/km). The Irsic et al. limit drops to 4.1 keV when restricted to k_max<0.1 s/km and earlier thermal-history priors. The dominant systematics are now IGM peculiar velocities, inhomogeneous reionization and the thermal history, rather than statistics alone. For non-resonantly produced (Dodelson-Widrow, DW) sterile neutrinos, these limits have to be converted to a sterile-neutrino mass through a transfer-function mapping. The commonly used relation from Viel et al. 2005 (astro-ph/0501562), quoted from memory and not checked against a retrieved full text, is m_s ~ 4.43 keV (m_th/keV)^{4/3} (omega_dm/0.1225)^{-1/3}. It turns 3.1-5.7 keV thermal-relic limits into roughly 20-45 keV DW limits, which are far above the masses that X-ray decay bounds allow for DW sterile neutrinos making up all of the dark matter. Pure DW production is therefore excluded as 100% of the dark matter, so the open questions are mixed cold-plus-warm scenarios (a sterile fraction below 1, constrained in 0812.0010 and 2504.06367), resonant production, and DW contributions on top of other production channels (1512.05369). Warning: no sterile-neutrino production-fraction tool was available in this toolset, so those fractions still need to be computed.

Quantities worth checking: DW sterile mass equivalent to each thermal-relic limit, using m_s ~ 4.43 keV (m_th/keV)^{4/3} (omega_dm/0.1225)^{-1/3}: about 20 keV (3.1), 22 keV (3.3), 29 keV (4.1) and 45 keV (5.7). These are rough figures; they should be checked against the paper and against alternative mappings such as half-mode-matching fits.; Half-mode wavenumber k_hm and half-mode mass for each limit, compared between the thermal-relic and DW transfer functions.; DW relic abundance Omega_s h^2 as a function of (m_s, sin^2 2theta), and the mixing angle needed for Omega_s = Omega_dm, compared with X-ray decay limits.; Production fraction f_s = Omega_s/Omega_dm allowed by cold-plus-warm Lyman-alpha bounds (0812.0010, 2504.06367) along the X-ray-allowed mixing angles.; Average momentum <p/T> of the DW spectrum (about 3.15 times the active-neutrino temperature, with g* corrections), used to check the mapping..

**Plan** — 4 lines of investigation:
1. Use the sterile-neutrino server to compute non-resonant (Dodelson-Widrow) production: the relic abundance Omega_s h^2 and the production fraction f_s = Omega_s/Omega_dm across the (m_s, sin^2 2theta) plane. Find the mixing angle at which f_s = 1, and compare that line with the X-ray decay bounds and the Lyman-alpha DW mass floors (about 20, 22, 29 and 45 keV, from thermal-relic limits of 3.1, 3.3, 4.1 and 5.7 keV). — The task explicitly asks for the sterile-nu tools to supply production fractions. The survey flagged these fractions as not yet computed, and they are the core of the comparison with non-resonant production.
2. Verify the recent Lyman-alpha WDM thermal-relic limits and their stated systematics against full texts, with citable quotes. Extract the cold-plus-warm bounds on the warm fraction as a function of mass from 0812.0010 and 2504.06367. — The survey's limits were not quote-checked. The bounds on the warm fraction are needed to judge which d-01 production fractions are allowed.
3. Cross-check the mapping from thermal-relic mass to DW sterile-neutrino mass. Verify the Viel et al. 2005 formula and its coefficient against the full text, gather alternative mappings (half-mode matching, the 2007.13751 framework, Abazajian-style relations), and quantify how much the DW mass floors change between mappings. — Comparing Lyman-alpha limits with DW production depends on this conversion. The relation was quoted from memory, and the choice of mapping can shift the floors by tens of percent.
4. Obtain quote-verified X-ray upper limits on sin^2 2theta versus m_s for keV sterile neutrinos over roughly 5-50 keV. Use them to define 'X-ray-allowed mixing' for d-01 and to test whether 100% DW dark matter is excluded independently of Lyman-alpha. — No listed tool provides observational X-ray limits, and no key paper is dedicated to them. Without them, the central exclusion claim and the f_s values at the X-ray limit are unverifiable. (added by the critic)
Critic's view: revise — The server is an SBBN/N_eff tool (serve-sbbn.sh), and the brief says no production-fraction tool was available. Do not assume it returns Omega_s h^2 or f_s for keV DW production. Make step 1 a go/no-go gate. If describe_sterile_nu_tools shows no DW relic-abundance output, or a validity range that excludes 1-100 keV, stop. Report the gap and do not build tables from proxies such as N_eff or BBN shifts. Write tool-derived f_s only when a tool actually returned it.; predict_sterile_nu_xray_line predicts the line energy and flux. It does not give an observational upper limit on sin^2 2theta. 'X-ray-allowed mixing' therefore needs a literature bound (see the added direction) unless describe shows the tool holds X-ray limit data. Otherwise the f_s values at the X-ray limit cannot be verified.; Step 7 is circular. The Lyman-alpha DW floors of about 20-45 keV apply only to f_s = 1. For f_s < 1, the relevant constraint is the mixed cold-plus-warm bound from d-02, converted with the mapping from d-03. Make the f_s table the comparison of tool f_s against the d-02 maximum warm fraction at each mass, and state this dependency. Also, the 7.1 keV, 7e-11 point should give f_s much less than 1 under pure DW. Treat it as a check against the expected small fraction, not as an f_s = 1 check..

**Wave 1** — now exploring, in parallel: Use the sterile-neutrino server to compute non-resonant (Dodelson-Widrow) production: the relic abundance Omega_s h^2 and the production fraction f_s = Omega_s/Omega_dm across the (m_s, sin^2 2theta) plane. Find the mixing angle at which f_s = 1, and compare that line with the X-ray decay bounds and the Lyman-alpha DW mass floors (about 20, 22, 29 and 45 keV, from thermal-relic limits of 3.1, 3.3, 4.1 and 5.7 keV).; Verify the recent Lyman-alpha WDM thermal-relic limits and their stated systematics against full texts, with citable quotes. Extract the cold-plus-warm bounds on the warm fraction as a function of mass from 0812.0010 and 2504.06367.; Obtain quote-verified X-ray upper limits on sin^2 2theta versus m_s for keV sterile neutrinos over roughly 5-50 keV. Use them to define 'X-ray-allowed mixing' for d-01 and to test whether 100% DW dark matter is excluded independently of Lyman-alpha..

**Finding:** The sterile-nu server gives DW Omega_s h^2 proportional to sin^2 2theta. At sin^2 2theta = 1e-12 it returns Omega_s h^2 = 0.003041 (20 keV), 0.00361 (22 keV), 0.005936 (29 keV), 0.01309 (45 keV) and 0.0004715 (7.1 keV). Linear scaling to f_s = Omega_s h^2/0.12 = 1 then gives sin^2 2theta(f_s=1) of about 3.95e-11, 3.32e-11, 2.02e-11, 9.17e-12 and 2.55e-10 respectively. At the 3.5 keV line point (7.1 keV, 7e-11) the tool gives Omega_s h^2 = 0.033, i.e. f_s = 0.275.

**Finding:** At the DW f_s = 1 mixing, the tool's X-ray check gives: 20 keV with sin^2 2theta = 3.95e-11 is EXCLUDED by NuSTAR M31 (Roach+ 2020); 29 keV (2.02e-11) and 45 keV (9.17e-12) are 'not excluded', but only because no tabulated limit lies within 30% in mass. Those two masses are uncovered by the tool, not shown to be allowed. The tool also does not return the numerical limit on sin^2 2theta, so f_s at the X-ray limit cannot be read directly from it.

**Finding:** A DW scan of 6400 points over m_s = 1-100 keV and sin^2 2theta = 1e-14 to 1e-6 gives 3092 overclosing points (Omega_s h^2 > 0.12) and 968 BBN-excluded points. BBN is weak for keV DW: the largest BBN-allowed mixing is 3.03e-8 at 26.2 keV and 1.5e-8 at 49.7 keV, about 3 orders of magnitude above the f_s = 1 line. BBN therefore does not constrain DW dark matter; only X-ray limits and Lyman-alpha do. The exclusion plot is Figure 25.

**Finding:** NuSTAR X-ray line searches give the leading upper limits on sin^2 2theta for keV sterile neutrinos over 10-50 keV. Perez et al. 2016 (arXiv:1609.00667, Galactic Center 0-bounce) state: "In most of the mass range 10–50 keV, these are now the strongest limits, at some masses improving upon previous limits by a factor of ∼ 10". Roach et al. 2020 (arXiv:1908.09037, Galactic bulge) find "no evidence of anomalous x-ray lines in the energy range 5–20 keV, corresponding to sterile neutrino masses 10–40 keV". In 1609.00667 Fig. 1 the limits are plotted on a sin^2 2theta axis running from 1e-15 to 1e-7; the curve values were not digitised here.

**Finding:** Quote-checked thermal-relic Lyman-alpha limits (95% CL / 2 sigma). Irsic et al. 2023 (2309.04533): m_WDM > 5.7 keV from HIRES+UVES at z = 4.2-5.0 with k_max = 0.2 s/km. Restricting to k_max < 0.1 s/km with earlier thermal-history priors gives 4.1 keV. The main small-scale modelling systematics are IGM peculiar-velocity structure and inhomogeneous reionization. Villasenor et al. 2022 (2209.14220): m_WDM > 3.1 keV, likelihood peak at 4.5 keV, from 1080 Cholla simulations against Boera+2019 data at 4.0 < z < 5.2; the suppression saturates at k > 0.1 s/km because of peculiar-velocity smearing. Viel et al. 2013 (1306.2314): m_WDM > 3.3 keV from 25 z > 4 HIRES/MIKE quasars. Irsic et al. 2017 (1702.01764): XQ-100 (z = 3-4.2) alone 1.4 keV, HIRES/MIKE (z = 4.2-5.4) re-analysis 4.1 keV, combined 5.3 keV, assuming a power-law T(z); allowing sudden temperature jumps of up to 5000 K lowers the combined limit to 3.5 keV.

**Finding:** Cold-plus-warm bounds. Garcia-Gallego et al. 2025 (2504.06367; Sherwood-Relics with a neural-network emulator; UVES+HIRES at z = 4.2-5.0) give f_WDM < 0.16, 0.35, 0.50 and 0.67 (2 sigma) for THERMAL-RELIC masses m_WDM = 1, 2, 3 and 4 keV. Boyarsky et al. 2008 (0812.0010; WMAP5 + SDSS/VHS Lyman-alpha) state their bounds in terms of the NON-RESONANTLY PRODUCED sterile-neutrino mass. In the pure-WDM case they find m_nrp >= 8 keV (frequentist 99.7%) or 12.1 keV (Bayesian 95%). For 5 keV < m_nrp < infinity any mass is allowed when F_wdm < 0.6 (frequentist 99.7%) or F_wdm < 0.35 (Bayesian 95%).

**Finding:** Merle 2017 (arXiv:1702.08430, quote verified) says that non-resonant Dodelson-Widrow production is "nowadays known to be excluded by observations", because "the resulting spectrum would feature too many particles with rather large momenta, making this setting similar to a hot DM case and thus excluded by data". This statement rests on structure formation combined with X-ray bounds; the review does not make an X-ray-only exclusion claim.

**Completed — Use the sterile-neutrino server to compute non-resonant (Dodelson-Widrow) production: the relic abundance Omega_s h^2 and the production fraction f_s = Omega_s/Omega_dm across the (m_s, sin^2 2theta) plane. Find the mixing angle at which f_s = 1, and compare that line with the X-ray decay bounds and the Lyman-alpha DW mass floors (about 20, 22, 29 and 45 keV, from thermal-relic limits of 3.1, 3.3, 4.1 and 5.7 keV)..** Pure DW sterile neutrinos at 20 keV cannot be all of the dark matter under this tool's physics: the tool's own X-ray check (NuSTAR M31, Roach+ 2020) excludes the f_s = 1 point. At 29 and 45 keV the tool cannot decide either way, because it has no X-ray limit near those masses; the 'not excluded' flag there means no coverage, not allowed. The success criteria are only partly met. The f_s = 1 mixings and the plot are done, but the X-ray limit on sin^2 2theta and f_s at that limit are missing: the tool returns only an excluded/not-excluded flag from sparse tabulated points, never a numerical limit (finding f-002, question q-06). It assumes pure Dodelson-Widrow (DW) production, with Shi-Fuller resonant production as a separate option (this answers q-01). It reports Omega_s h^2, Delta N_eff, lifetime and free-streaming length, but not f_s directly and not k_hm (finding f-001).

Check at the 3.5 keV line point (7.1 keV, sin^2 2theta = 7e-11): Omega_s h^2 = 0.033, so f_s = 0.275 (tc-...-23).

Omega_s h^2 scales linearly with sin^2 2theta, which the 374-point grid confirms. At sin^2 2theta = 1e-12 the tool gives Omega_s h^2 = 0.003041 (20 keV), 0.00361 (22 keV), 0.005936 (29 keV) and 0.01309 (45 keV) (tc-...-31). Scaling to Omega_s h^2 = 0.12 gives the mixing for f_s = 1. This rescaling is my own arithmetic, not a direct tool output.

| m_s | sin^2 2theta at f_s = 1 | Tool X-ray check at that mixing |
|---|---|---|
| 20 keV | 3.95e-11 | Excluded by NuSTAR M31 (tc-...-33) |
| 22 keV | 3.32e-11 | Not run |
| 29 keV | 2.02e-11 | No tabulated limit within 30% in mass, so undecided (tc-...-35) |
| 45 keV | 9.17e-12 | No tabulated limit within 30% in mass, so undecided (tc-...-34) |
| 7.1 keV | 2.55e-10 | Not run (scaled from the same grid) |

Because there are no numerical X-ray limits, I cannot give f_s at the maximal X-ray-allowed mixing, or the fraction that remains allowed, at the four Lyman-alpha floors. This needs d-04's numerical limits: f_s,max = sin^2 2theta_X / sin^2 2theta(f_s=1).

BBN does not matter here. A 6400-point DW scan over 1-100 keV and sin^2 2theta = 1e-14 to 1e-6 found 3092 overclosing points and 968 BBN-excluded points. The largest BBN-allowed mixing is about 3e-8 near 26 keV and 1.5e-8 near 50 keV, roughly 3 orders of magnitude above the f_s = 1 line (f-003).

Files are in /Users/nramachandra/hep-genesis-testing/projects/ramp-research-lyman-wdm/runs/261019_110120/:
- Exclusion plot (Figure 25): exclusion_scan_DW_d94a06.png and exclusion_scan_DW_d94a06.pdf
- Scan: scan_DW_d94a06.npz and scan_DW_d94a06.csv
- Grids: sterile_nu_grid_DW_4bbf6a.csv (374 points) and sterile_nu_grid_DW_a74034.csv (12 masses at sin^2 2theta = 1e-12)

Findings f-001, f-002 and f-003 and question q-06 are posted on the board.

**Blocked — Obtain quote-verified X-ray upper limits on sin^2 2theta versus m_s for keV sterile neutrinos over roughly 5-50 keV. Use them to define 'X-ray-allowed mixing' for d-01 and to test whether 100% DW dark matter is excluded independently of Lyman-alpha..** (The tool budget ran out before any numerical limits were extracted. The 1908.09037 text failed to decode at offset 48000, so its limit section could not be read. The next steps are to read the results sections of 1609.00667 and 1901.01262, or to use predict_sterile_nu_xray_line at 7, 20, 30 and 45 keV along the f_s = 1 mixing line from d-01.) Half the success criteria are met. (1) Literature statement on pure DW, quote verified: Merle 2017 (arXiv:1702.08430) says non-resonant (DW) production is 'nowadays known to be excluded by observations', because its spectrum is 'similar to a hot DM case and thus excluded by data'. That rests on structure formation combined with X-ray bounds, not on X-ray limits alone (finding f-007). (2) X-ray limits, verbal statements only, quote verified: NuSTAR Galactic Center (Perez et al., arXiv:1609.00667) gives 'the strongest limits' over most of 10-50 keV; NuSTAR Galactic bulge (Roach et al., arXiv:1908.09037) finds no lines at 5-20 keV, i.e. m_s = 10-40 keV (finding f-004). Fig. 1 of 1609.00667 plots the limits on a sin^2 2theta axis from 1e-15 to 1e-7, but no curve values were read. All three papers are cited in /Users/nramachandra/hep-genesis-testing/projects/ramp-research-lyman-wdm/runs/261019_110120/references.bib, with full texts saved in the same directory. Not yet established: the table of sin^2 2theta limits at about 7, 20, 30 and 45 keV, and whether 100% DW dark matter is excluded by X-ray limits alone (question q-07).

**Completed — Verify the recent Lyman-alpha WDM thermal-relic limits and their stated systematics against full texts, with citable quotes. Extract the cold-plus-warm bounds on the warm fraction as a function of mass from 0812.0010 and 2504.06367..** Thermal-relic limits checked (f-005, tc-...-36/45/46/47). 2309.04533 (checked against the full text): m_WDM > 5.7 keV (95% CL) from HIRES+UVES at z = 4.2-5.0 with k_max = 0.2 s/km; restricting to k_max < 0.1 s/km with earlier thermal-history priors gives 4.1 keV. Its main small-scale systematics are IGM peculiar velocities and inhomogeneous reionization, and it says the thermal-history uncertainty now matters less. The other three were checked against their arXiv abstracts only, not the full texts: 2209.14220 gives > 3.1 keV with a likelihood peak at 4.5 keV (4.0 < z < 5.2, Boera+2019 data, suppression saturates at k > 0.1 s/km); 1306.2314 gives > 3.3 keV from 25 z > 4 HIRES/MIKE quasars; 1702.01764 gives XQ-100 1.4 keV, HIRES/MIKE 4.1 keV and combined 5.3 keV assuming a power-law T(z), or 3.5 keV if temperature jumps of 5000 K are allowed. Mixed-DM bounds (f-006): 2504.06367 gives f_WDM < 0.16, 0.35, 0.50, 0.67 (2 sigma) at thermal-relic masses 1, 2, 3, 4 keV (so these are thermal-relic bounds, answering q-02). 0812.0010 is expressed directly in the non-resonant (DW) sterile mass: pure-WDM limits are m_nrp >= 8 keV (99.7%) and 12.1 keV (Bayesian 95%), and any mass above 5 keV is allowed if F_wdm < 0.6 (99.7%) or F_wdm < 0.35 (Bayesian 95%). The 2504.06367 masses mapped to DW masses of about 4.4, 11, 18 and 28 keV are my own estimate from the unverified Viel 2005 formula, not a tool result. Not done: digitized fraction-versus-mass curves (dead end x-01: the HTML for 2504.06367 only gave its Figs 1 and 4, board Figures 7 and 8, which are not constraint plots; the 0812.0010 fraction panels Figs 7, 12, 13 are at /Users/nramachandra/hep-genesis-testing/projects/ramp-research-lyman-wdm/runs/261019_110120/figures_0812.0010/ only partly, Figs 12-13 were not downloaded), the 2023-2025 search for newer limits, and full-text k_max and prior details for 2209.14220, 1306.2314 and 1702.01764. Bibliography: references.bib in the run directory holds 2309.04533, 2504.06367 and 0812.0010.

**Critic, wave 1** — continue: 6 findings stand up to the evidence, 1 questioned ('At the DW f_s = 1 mixing, the tool's X-ray check gives: 20 keV with sin^2 2theta = 3.95e-1': None of the quoted excerpts (tc-...-33, -34, -35) contains the central claim. They stop at the per-target flux lines, before any 'EXCLUDED by NuSTAR M31' or 'no tabulated limit within 30% in mass' text. tc-...-22 is only the skill-loading instructions. The exclusion verdict at 20 keV and the no-coverage verdict at 29 and 45 keV are therefore not shown in the evidence. The tool's flux model is also physically doubtful. It treats a 1e12 Msun halo at 8.3 kpc as a point source and returns 116 ph/s/cm^2 for the Milky Way centre, which is many orders of magnitude above any real field-of-view flux. Its M31 exclusion flag should not be trusted without comparison to the published limit.).

Issues: The tool's DW normalisation has not been cross-checked. The common Abazajian-type fit, Omega h^2 ~ 0.1 (sin^2 2theta / 3e-9)(m_s / 3 keV)^1.8, gives sin^2 2theta(f_s=1) of about 7-8e-10 at 7.1 keV. The tool's value is 2.55e-10, roughly a factor of 3 lower. DW abundance predictions differ by factors of a few in the literature (hadronic uncertainties, Asaka-Laine-Shaposhnikov). Any f_s,max derived from this line inherits that factor and must state the source of the normalisation.; The tc-...-31 excerpt shows only the 7.1 keV row. The 20, 22, 29 and 45 keV Omega_s h^2 values are not visible in the quoted evidence, although the arithmetic from them is internally consistent (0.12/0.003041 x 1e-12 = 3.95e-11, and so on). The full rows from sterile_nu_grid_DW_a74034.csv should be quoted.; The counts (968 BBN-excluded, 3092 overclosing) appear in the evidence. The maxima of the BBN-allowed mixing (3.03e-8 at 26.2 keV, 1.5e-8 at 49.7 keV) do not. Those mixings lie deep in the overclosed region, so 'BBN does not constrain DW DM' is correct but trivially so. The claim should say this..

**Next steps after wave 1** — One wave and 20 tool calls remain. d-03 (the mapping cross-check) has not run yet, so it is carried over and runs first. It is capped at about 6 calls: quote the Viel 2005 coefficient from astro-ph/0501562, quote one mapping with different exponents (for example a half-mode fit from 1702.01764 or Bozek et al.), and map the 1-4 keV thermal-relic masses to DW masses. d-04 is reopened because its blocker, running out of budget, has now been lifted. Its scope is the critic's numerical X-ray step: read the limit sections of 1609.00667 and 1901.01262 (retrying 1908.09037 from another offset if needed), tabulate sin^2 2theta_X at about 7, 20, 22, 29 and 45 keV with source and figure labels, and compute f_s,max from the d-01 f_s=1 mixings. That answers q-03, q-06 and q-07, and it should take about 7 calls. I am not adding a duplicate X-ray direction. The single new direction covers the DW-normalisation cross-check the critic flagged, which is roughly a factor of 3 at 7.1 keV, and it builds the final allowed-fraction table so the run ends with the comparison the task requested. The task did not ask for facility runs and all compute is lightweight local or hosted work, so no facility dispatch is needed (q-05). No directions are closed: d-01 and d-02 are already closed, and the remaining work is all finishing work on the central question.

New lines of investigation: Cross-check the sterile-nu server's Dodelson-Widrow relic-abundance normalisation against at least two quote-verified published DW yield formulas. Propagate the spread to sin^2 2theta(f_s=1) at 7.1, 20, 22, 29 and 45 keV. Then assemble the final comparison table: allowed DW fraction versus sterile mass from Lyman-alpha mixed-DM bounds and from X-ray limits, with the binding constraint marked at each mass..

**Wave 2** — now exploring, in parallel: Cross-check the mapping from thermal-relic mass to DW sterile-neutrino mass. Verify the Viel et al. 2005 formula and its coefficient against the full text, gather alternative mappings (half-mode matching, the 2007.13751 framework, Abazajian-style relations), and quantify how much the DW mass floors change between mappings.; Obtain quote-verified X-ray upper limits on sin^2 2theta versus m_s for keV sterile neutrinos over roughly 5-50 keV. Use them to define 'X-ray-allowed mixing' for d-01 and to test whether 100% DW dark matter is excluded independently of Lyman-alpha.; Cross-check the sterile-nu server's Dodelson-Widrow relic-abundance normalisation against at least two quote-verified published DW yield formulas. Propagate the spread to sin^2 2theta(f_s=1) at 7.1, 20, 22, 29 and 45 keV. Then assemble the final comparison table: allowed DW fraction versus sterile mass from Lyman-alpha mixed-DM bounds and from X-ray limits, with the binding constraint marked at each mass..

**Finding:** Roach et al. 2022 (arXiv:2207.04572, NuSTAR Milky Way halo, about 7 Ms/detector blank-sky plus about 20 Ms/detector stacked data) find no anomalous lines and set sin^2(2theta) limits for m_s = 6-40 keV. Quote: "we strongly disfavor a ~7-keV sterile neutrino decaying into a 3.5-keV photon" and "we derive leading limits on sterile neutrinos with masses ~15–18 keV and ~25–40 keV, reaching or extending below the big bang nucleosynthesis limit". The conclusions add that the parameter space "is now mostly covered", but this "does not fully rule out sterile neutrinos as the only DM component"; it shows "the simple and elegant mixing production mechanism [8, 9] may be insufficient". The authors therefore do NOT claim that X-ray data alone exclude 100% DW dark matter. Their "mostly covered" statement relies on adding satellite-counting bounds.

**Finding:** Roach et al. 2020 (arXiv:1908.09037, NuSTAR Galactic bulge, about 190 ks) give 95% one-sided limits on the decay rate Gamma for m_s = 10-40 keV, quoted in Gamma [s^-1] rather than sin^2 2theta. Their Fig. 5 plots these limits on a Gamma axis spanning 1e-29 to 1e-27 s^-1, compared with Neronov+2016, Perez+2017 and Ng+2019. The paper states the limits are "comparable to previous NuSTAR limits" and improve on earlier ones by about 2x at 10-12 keV. They are weakened near m ~ 16 keV and 30-40 keV, where the background fit shows excesses. No numerical values were tabulated, and the curves were not digitised.

**Blocked — Obtain quote-verified X-ray upper limits on sin^2 2theta versus m_s for keV sterile neutrinos over roughly 5-50 keV. Use them to define 'X-ray-allowed mixing' for d-01 and to test whether 100% DW dark matter is excluded independently of Lyman-alpha..** (The numerical X-ray limits exist only in figures. Digitising them (get_paper_figures plus reading the curves) and adding 2207.04572 to references.bib did not fit in the tool budget, and NuSTAR does not cover 45 keV.) Half the success criteria are met: the literature statements on whether pure Dodelson-Widrow (DW) production can be all of the dark matter are quote-verified, but the numerical table of X-ray limits on sin^2 2theta could not be built. (1) Literature statements, all quote-verified. Merle 2017 (arXiv:1702.08430) says DW production is 'nowadays known to be excluded by observations'; that rests on structure formation together with X-ray bounds (f-007). Roach et al. 2022 (arXiv:2207.04572, NuSTAR Milky Way halo, about 7 and 20 Ms per detector) set sin^2 2theta limits for m_s = 6-40 keV. They 'strongly disfavor a ~7-keV sterile neutrino' (the 3.5 keV line candidate) and give leading limits at about 15-18 and 25-40 keV, 'reaching or extending below the big bang nucleosynthesis limit'. They also state that the parameter space is 'mostly covered' (this includes satellite-counting bounds), but that this 'does not fully rule out sterile neutrinos as the only DM component'; only the simple mixing production mechanism 'may be insufficient' (f-008). So no source makes a clean claim that X-ray limits alone exclude 100% DW dark matter. Roach et al. 2020 (arXiv:1908.09037) give 95% limits on the decay rate Gamma (not on sin^2 2theta) for 10-40 keV, plotted in their Fig. 5 on an axis of 1e-29 to 1e-27 s^-1. They are about 2x better at 10-12 keV and weaker near 16 keV and 30-40 keV (f-009). Perez et al. 2017 (arXiv:1609.00667) give the strongest limits over most of 10-50 keV (f-004). (2) Not established: numerical sin^2 2theta limits at 7, 20, 22, 29 and 45 keV, so the X-ray-allowed f_s,max for d-01 cannot be computed yet. The papers give the limits only as figure curves, which were not digitised (dead end x-02). NuSTAR coverage ends at 40 keV, so 45 keV needs INTEGRAL/SPI or Fermi-GBM limits. result.summary:
Pure DW sterile neutrinos at 20 keV cannot be all of the dark matter under this tool's physics: the tool's own X-ray check (NuSTAR M31, Roach+ 2020) excludes the f_s = 1 point. At 29 and 45 keV the tool cannot decide either way, because it has no X-ray limit near those masses; the 'not excluded' flag there means no coverage, not allowed. The success criteria are only partly met. The f_s = 1 mixings and the plot are done, but the X-ray limit on sin^2 2theta and f_s at that limit are missing: the tool returns only an excluded/not-excluded flag from sparse tabulated points, never a numerical limit (finding f-002, question q-06). It assumes pure Dodelson-Widrow (DW) production, with Shi-Fuller resonant production as a separate option (this answers q-01). It reports Omega_s h^2, Delta N_eff, lifetime and free-streaming length, but not f_s directly and not k_hm (finding f-001).

Check at the 3.5 keV line point (7.1 keV, sin^2 2theta = 7e-11): Omega_s h^2 = 0.033, so f_s = 0.275 (tc-...-23).

Omega_s h^2 scales linearly with sin^2 2theta, which the 374-point grid confirms. At sin^2 2theta = 1e-12 the tool gives Omega_s h^2 = 0.003041 (20 keV), 0.00361 (22 keV), 0.005936 (29 keV) and 0.01309 (45 keV) (tc-...-31). Scaling to Omega_s h^2 = 0.12 gives the mixing for f_s = 1. This rescaling is my own arithmetic, not a direct tool output.

| m_s | sin^2 2theta at f_s = 1 | Tool X-ray check at that mixing |
|---|---|---|

messages.report:
# Lyman-alpha forest constraints on warm dark matter compared with non-resonant (Dodelson-Widrow) sterile-neutrino production

## Abstract

We checked the recent high-redshift Lyman-alpha forest lower limits on the thermal-relic warm dark matter (WDM) mass against the papers. The values are 3.1, 3.3 and 5.7 keV (95% CL), and 4.1 keV for the scale-restricted variant of the strongest analysis. We converted them to non-resonant (Dodelson-Widrow, DW) sterile-neutrino mass floors with the Viel et al. 2005 relation, now verified against its full text. The floors are about 20, 22, 29 and 45 keV.

A sterile-neutrino tool server computed the DW relic abundance Omega_s h^2 as a function of (m_s, sin^2 2theta). From this we obtained the mixing at which DW sterile neutrinos make up all of the dark matter (f_s = 1) at each floor:

| m_s | sin^2 2theta at f_s = 1 |
|---|---|
| 20 keV | 3.95e-11 |
| 22 keV | 3.32e-11 |
| 29 keV | 2.02e-11 |
| 45 keV | 9.17e-12 |

The tool's normalisation produces 3 to 16 times more DW dark matter per unit mixing than two published yield fits. This makes the production fraction uncertain by that factor. At the 3.5 keV line point the fraction is f_s = 0.275 (tool), 0.089 or 0.023 (published fits).

The tool's coarse X-ray check excludes f_s = 1 at 20 keV. At 29 and 45 keV it has no coverage and cannot decide. Numerical X-ray limits on sin^2 2theta were not obtained, so the central comparison is incomplete: the maximum DW fraction allowed by X-rays at each Lyman-alpha floor could not be computed. On the evidence gathered here, we cannot show that 100% DW dark matter is excluded once Lyman-alpha and X-ray constraints are combined.

## Background

The Lyman-alpha flux power spectrum at z ~ 4-5 probes the small-scale suppression caused by WDM free-streaming. The limits have tightened over time:

- **Narayanan et al. 2000 (arXiv:astro-ph/0005095):** m_WDM > 750 eV, the historical baseline.
- **Viel et al. 2013 (arXiv:1306.2314):** benchmark limit of m_WDM > 3.3 keV (2 sigma) from 25 HIRES/MIKE quasars at z > 4.
- **Irsic et al. 2017 (arXiv:1702.01764):** combined XQ-100 with HIRES/MIKE.
- **Villasenor et al. 2022 (arXiv:2209.14220):** independent analysis using 1080 Cholla simulations.
- **Irsic et al. 2023 (arXiv:2309.04533):** the current strongest bound. It names IGM peculiar velocities and inhomogeneous reionization as the leading small-scale systematics.

These are thermal-relic limits. Applying them to DW sterile neutrinos needs a mass mapping. The standard one is from Viel et al. 2005 (arXiv:astro-ph/0501562). Emulator frameworks for general non-cold spectra exist (arXiv:2007.13751) but do not supply a DW-specific relation.

Mixed cold-plus-warm models are constrained as a function of the warm fraction:

- Boyarsky et al. 2008 (arXiv:0812.0010), stated in the DW mass itself.
- Garcia-Gallego et al. 2025 (arXiv:2504.06367), stated in thermal-relic mass.

On the particle side, Merle's 2017 review (arXiv:1702.08430) describes DW production as excluded by observations. arXiv:1512.05369 treats DW on top of other production channels. NuSTAR line searches set the leading X-ray limits over roughly 10-50 keV:

- Perez et al., arXiv:1609.00667.
- Roach et al. 2020, arXiv:1908.09037.
- Roach et al. 2022, arXiv:2207.04572.

## Results

### Thermal-relic Lyman-alpha limits

The limits were checked against the full text for arXiv:2309.04533 and against the abstracts for the others.

- **Irsic et al. 2023 (arXiv:2309.04533):** m_WDM > 5.7 keV (95% CL). It uses HIRES+UVES data at z = 4.2-5.0 with k_max = 0.2 s/km. Restricting to k_max < 0.1 s/km with earlier thermal-history priors gives 4.1 keV. The main small-scale modelling systematics are IGM peculiar velocities and inhomogeneous reionization. The paper says the thermal-history uncertainty now matters less.
- **Villasenor et al. 2022 (arXiv:2209.14220):** m_WDM > 3.1 keV, with a likelihood peak at 4.5 keV. It uses Boera et al. 2019 data at 4.0 < z < 5.2. The suppression saturates at k > 0.1 s/km because of peculiar-velocity smearing.
- **Viel et al. 2013 (arXiv:1306.2314):** m_WDM > 3.3 keV from 25 HIRES/MIKE quasars at z > 4.
- **Irsic et al. 2017 (arXiv:1702.01764):**
  - XQ-100 alone (z = 3-4.2) gives 1.4 keV.
  - Re-analysed HIRES/MIKE gives 4.1 keV.
  - The combination gives 5.3 keV, assuming a power-law T(z).
  - Allowing sudden temperature jumps of up to 5000 K lowers the combined limit to 3.5 keV.

The k_max and prior details of the three abstract-only papers were not checked against their full texts.

### Mapping thermal-relic limits to DW mass

Eq. (5) of Viel et al. 2005 was verified in the full text:

m_sterile = 4.43 keV (m_thermal / 1 keV)^{4/3} (0.25 (0.7)^2 / omega_x)^{1/3}

The normalisation 0.25 x 0.49 = 0.1225 matches the brief. The relation follows from equating omega_x and m_x/T_x for a thermal relic and a sterile neutrino "which share the same phase-space distribution but with an overall suppression factor chi". The DW spectrum is therefore treated as a rescaled Fermi-Dirac distribution, and the thermal and DW transfer functions are identical by construction.

DW floors from our own arithmetic:

| Thermal-relic limit | DW floor, omega_dm = 0.12 | DW floor, omega_dm = 0.1225 |
|---|---|---|
| 3.1 keV | 20.2 keV | 20.0 keV |
| 3.3 keV | 21.9 keV | 21.8 keV |
| 4.1 keV | 29.3 keV | 29.1 keV |
| 5.7 keV | 45.4 keV | 45.1 keV |

These confirm the brief's rough values to within 1%. Using the 4.1 keV variant instead of 5.7 keV lowers the DW floor from about 45 keV to about 29 keV. This is the size of the effect of restricting scales and priors.

**Transfer-function fit.** Viel 2005 fits T(k) = [1 + (alpha k)^{2nu}]^{-5/nu}, with nu = 1.12, for k < 5 h/Mpc. For thermal relics, alpha = 0.049 (m_x/keV)^{-1.11} (Omega_x/0.25)^{0.11} (h/0.7)^{1.22} h^-1 Mpc. Setting T^2 = 1/2 gives k_hm = 0.325/alpha (our arithmetic). For 3.1, 3.3, 4.1 and 5.7 keV this gives:

| Thermal-relic limit | alpha (h^-1 Mpc) | k_hm (h/Mpc) |
|---|---|---|
| 3.1 keV | 0.01396 | about 23.3 |
| 3.3 keV | 0.01302 | about 25.0 |
| 4.1 keV | 0.01024 | about 31.8 |
| 5.7 keV | 0.00710 | about 45.8 |

These lie far outside the k < 5 h/Mpc range on which the fit was calibrated. The critic did not consider the k_hm values settled, because they are an extrapolation and were not recomputed against the half-mode mass of about 2x10^8 Msun/h quoted in arXiv:1306.2314. Under Viel's mapping the DW k_hm is identical by construction, so this calculation does not test the mapping itself.

**The arXiv:2007.13751 framework.** It uses T(k) = [1 + (alpha k)^beta]^gamma. This reduces to the Viel form for beta = 2nu and gamma = -5/nu. A 2 keV WDM is fitted by [alpha, beta, gamma] = [0.02, 2.2, -4.5]. In the sections read, it gives no DW relation. Using it for DW would require fitting these parameters to a Boltzmann-code DW transfer function, which was not possible without CLASS/CAMB.

No second, independent mapping was verified, so the spread between mappings is unknown.

### DW abundance from the sterile-neutrino tool

The server models pure DW production, with Shi-Fuller resonant production available as a separate option. It returns:

- Omega_s h^2
- Delta N_eff
- BBN observables
- lifetime
- free-streaming length

It does not return k_hm. Contrary to the brief's warning, the tool does return relic abundances, so f_s = Omega_s h^2 / 0.12 is tool-derived. The rescaling to f_s = 1 below is our own arithmetic.

Omega_s h^2 scales linearly with sin^2 2theta; a 374-point grid confirmed this. At sin^2 2theta = 1e-12 the tool gives the values below, and linear scaling gives the f_s = 1 mixings:

| m_s | Omega_s h^2 at sin^2 2theta = 1e-12 | sin^2 2theta at f_s = 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 7.1 keV | 0.000471462 | 2.55e-10 |
| 20 keV | 0.00304114 | 3.95e-11 |
| 22 keV | 0.00361029 | 3.32e-11 |
| 29 keV | 0.00593606 | 2.02e-11 |
| 45 keV | 0.0130907 | 9.17e-12 |

As a direct check at the 3.5 keV line point (7.1 keV, sin^2 2theta = 7e-11), the tool returns Omega_s h^2 = 0.033, so f_s = 0.275.

### Cross-check of the DW normalisation

Two published DW yield fits were read in full text. They are quoted in the findings, but the citation step that validates quotes was not run for them.

- **Abazajian 2006 (astro-ph/0511630), Eq. 7:** m_s = 3.40 keV (sin^2 2theta / 1e-8)^-0.615 (Omega_DM / 0.26)^0.5, for T_QCD = 170 MeV and electron flavour.
- **Asaka-Laine-Shaposhnikov (hep-ph/0612182, Sec. 7.1):** the "most conservative" line, log10 sin^2 2theta = -7.6195 - 1.7428 log10(M/keV). The paper states this fit for M <= 4 keV, so using it here is an extrapolation. It is an overclosure upper line, so its ratio to the tool is a lower limit on the discrepancy.

Inverted to give the f_s = 1 mixing at the five masses:

| m_s | Tool | Abazajian 2006 (ratio to tool) | Asaka-Laine-Shaposhnikov (ratio to tool) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.1 keV | 2.55e-10 | 3.02e-9 (11.9) | 7.88e-10 (3.10) |
| 20 keV | 3.95e-11 | 5.61e-10 (14.2) | 1.30e-10 (3.29) |
| 22 keV | 3.32e-11 | 4.80e-10 (14.4) | 1.10e-10 (3.31) |
| 29 keV | 2.02e-11 | 3.06e-10 (15.2) | 6.79e-11 (3.36) |
| 45 keV | 9.17e-12 | 1.50e-10 (16.4) | 3.16e-11 (3.44) |

The tool therefore produces about 3 to 16 times more DW dark matter per unit mixing than these fits. At the 3.5 keV line point, f_s is:

- 0.275 with the tool,
- 0.089 with the Asaka-Laine-Shaposhnikov line,
- 0.023 with Abazajian 2006.

The tool is the most generous of the three. Its X-ray exclusion of f_s = 1 at 20 keV can therefore only get stronger under the published normalisations. Both the factor and its consequences were contested by the critic. The critic asks that the factor be settled with a modern DW calculation valid at 10-50 keV, rather than fits extrapolated from lower masses.

### X-ray status of the f_s = 1 points

The tool's X-ray check returns only an excluded/not-excluded flag based on sparse tabulated points. It gives no numerical limit on sin^2 2theta.

- **20 keV, sin^2 2theta = 3.95e-11:** excluded by the tool's tabulated NuSTAR M31 point, which the tool attributes to Roach et al. 2020.
- **29 keV (2.02e-11) and 45 keV (9.17e-12):** reported "not excluded", but only because no tabulated limit lies within 30% in mass. This means no coverage, not allowed.
- **22 keV:** not run.

The critic marked this result as needing independent confirmation, because it rests on the tool's coarse tabulation.

From the literature, with quotes verified:

- **Perez et al. (arXiv:1609.00667):** "In most of the mass range 10–50 keV, these are now the strongest limits". The curves are plotted on a sin^2 2theta axis from 1e-15 to 1e-7.
- **Roach et al. 2020 (arXiv:1908.09037):** find no anomalous lines at 5-20 keV, corresponding to m_s = 10-40 keV. Their limits are given on the decay rate Gamma, plotted on a 1e-29 to 1e-27 s^-1 axis. They are about 2x better than earlier limits at 10-12 keV, and weaker near 16 keV and 30-40 keV, where the background fit shows excesses. This reading was contested by the critic and is not independently verified.
- **Roach et al. 2022 (arXiv:2207.04572):** use about 7 Ms per detector of blank-sky data plus about 20 Ms per detector of stacked data. They "strongly disfavor a ~7-keV sterile neutrino" and give leading limits at about 15-18 and 25-40 keV, "reaching or extending below the big bang nucleosynthesis limit". They also state that this "does not fully rule out sterile neutrinos as the only DM component", only that "the simple and elegant mixing production mechanism … may be insufficient". Their statement that the parameter space is "mostly covered" includes satellite-counting bounds.

No numerical sin^2 2theta limits were extracted at 7, 20, 22, 29 or 45 keV, because the papers give them only as figure curves. NuSTAR coverage ends at 40 keV, so 45 keV would need INTEGRAL/SPI or Fermi-GBM limits.

### BBN in the DW plane

A 6400-point DW scan covered m_s = 1-100 keV and sin^2 2theta = 1e-14 to 1e-6. It found 3092 overclosing points (Omega_s h^2 > 0.12) and 968 points excluded by BBN at 95%.

[[FIGURE 25]]

Figure 25 shows the resulting exclusion map. The largest BBN-allowed mixing is 3.03e-8 at 26.2 keV and 1.5e-8 at 49.7 keV. This is about three orders of magnitude above the f_s = 1 line and deep in the overclosed region. BBN therefore does not constrain DW dark matter, but only trivially so; the relevant constraints are X-ray and Lyman-alpha. The two maximum-mixing values are not visible in the quoted tool output excerpt.

### Mixed cold-plus-warm bounds and the combined fraction table

**Garcia-Gallego et al. 2025 (arXiv:2504.06367).** This uses Sherwood-Relics simulations with a neural-network emulator and UVES+HIRES data at z = 4.2-5.0. It gives f_WDM < 0.16, 0.35, 0.50 and 0.67 (2 sigma) for thermal-relic masses of 1, 2, 3 and 4 keV.

**Boyarsky et al. 2008 (arXiv:0812.0010).** This is stated directly in the DW mass m_nrp:

- Pure WDM: m_nrp >= 8 keV (frequentist 99.7%) or 12.1 keV (Bayesian 95%).
- For any m_nrp above 5 keV, the model is allowed if F_wdm < 0.6 (99.7%) or F_wdm < 0.35 (Bayesian 95%).

- **45 keV:** f = 1 is allowed by Lyman-alpha even for the 5.7 keV variant.

The 0812.0010 figure files were downloaded, but none was analysed or digitised for this report. The extracted 2504.06367 figures are a simulation slice and an emulator schematic, not constraint plots, so they are not shown.

The Lyman-alpha side is now well characterised for thermal relics, and the Viel 2005 conversion to DW mass is confirmed in form and coefficient. The DW floors of roughly 20-45 keV are therefore reproducible under that convention.

Abstract: High resolution N-body simulations of cold dark matter (CDM) models predict that galaxies and clusters have cuspy halos with excessive substructure. Abstract: We present an analysis of high-resolution N-body simulations of decaying dark matter cosmologies focusing on the statistical properties of the transmitted Lyman-alpha forest flux in the high-redshift intergalactic medium. In this type of model a dark matter particle decays into a slightly less massive stable dark matter daughter particle and a comparably light particle. The small mass splitting provides a non-relativistic kick velocity V_k to the daughter particle resulting in free-streaming and subsequent damping of small-scale density fluctuations. Current Lyman-alpha forest power spectrum measurements probe comoving scales up to ~ 2-3 h^-1 Mpc at redshifts z ~ 2-4, providing one of the most robust ways to probe cosmological density fluctuations on relatively small scales. This is the most stringent model-independent bound on invisible dark matter decays with small mass splittings. For large mass splittings (large V_k), Lyman-alpha forest data restrict the dark matter lifetime to Gamma^-1 > 40 Gyr. Forthcoming BOSS data should be able to provide more stringent constraints on exotic dark matter, mainly because the larger BOSS quasar spectrum sample will significantly reduce statistical errors.

Title: General framework for cosmological dark matter bounds using $N$-body simulations
Authors: Keir K. Rogers, Hiranya V. Peiris

Abstract: We present a general framework for obtaining robust bounds on the nature of dark matter using cosmological $N$-body simulations and Lyman-alpha forest data. Abstract: We give an overview of the current status of keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter. After a short introduction, we start by a general discussion of non-thermal production of Dark Matter, which applies to the three most commonly discussed mechanisms to produce sterile neutrino Dark Matter in the Universe: non-resonant, resonant, and decay production. The main goal in each case is to compute the momentum distribution function $f(p,t)$, which incorporates the full information about the Dark Matter setting under consideration, at least in what concerns its cosmological aspects. While some difficulties lie in the actual computation of this quantity, it is decisive to obtain bounds from cosmic structure formation, which turn out to be the most crucial ones to distinguish different types of production. We will introduce these bounds and we put the resulting limits into a proper context, thereby illustrating that a significant amount of relevant parameter space is available, part of which is testable in particular by Lyman-$α$ data.

Abstract: The simplest way to create sterile neutrinos in the early Universe is by their admixture to active neutrinos. However, this mechanism, connected to the Dark Matter (DM) problem by Dodelson and Widrow (DW), cannot simultaneously meet the relic abundance constraint as well as bounds from structure formation and X-rays. Nonetheless, unless a symmetry forces active-sterile mixing to vanish exactly, the DW mechanism will unavoidably affect the sterile neutrino DM population created by any other production mechanism. We present a semi-analytic approach to the DW mechanism acting on an arbitrary initial abundance of sterile neutrinos, allowing to combine DW with any other preceding production mechanism in a physical and precise way. While previous analyses usually assumed that the spectra produced by DW and another mechanism can simply be added, we use our semi-analytic results to discuss the validity of this assumption and to quantify its accurateness, thereby also scrutinising the DW spectrum and the derived mass bounds. We then map our results to the case of sterile neutrino DM from the decay of a real SM singlet coupled to the Higgs. Finally, we will investigate aspects of structure formation beyond the usual simple free-streaming estimates in order to judge on the effects of the DW modification on the sterile neutrino DM spectra generated by scalar decay.

Abstract: We formulate an effective theory of structure formation (ETHOS) that enables cosmological structure formation to be computed in almost any microphysical model of dark matter physics. arXiv ID: 2309.04533
Title: Unveiling Dark Matter free-streaming at the smallest scales with high redshift Lyman-alpha forest
Authors: Vid Iršič, Matteo Viel, Martin G. Haehnelt, James S. Bolton, Margherita Molaro, Ewald Puchwein, Elisa Boera, George D. Becker, Prakash Gaikwad, Laura C. Keating, Girish Kulkarni
Year: 2023
Abstract: This study introduces novel constraints on the free-streaming of thermal relic warm dark matter (WDM) from Lyman-$α$ forest flux power spectra. Our analysis utilises a high-resolution, high-redshift sample of quasar spectra observed using the HIRES and UVES spectrographs ($z=4.2-5.0$). We employ a Bayesian inference framework and a simulation-based likelihood that encompasses various parameters including the free-streaming of dark matter, cosmological parameters, the thermal history of the intergalactic medium, and inhomogeneous reionization, to establish lower limits on the mass of a thermal relic WDM particle of $5.7\;\mathrm{keV}$ (at 95\% C.L.). arXiv ID: 2209.14220
Title: New Constraints on Warm Dark Matter from the Lyman-$α$ Forest Power Spectrum
Authors: Bruno Villasenor, Brant Robertson, Piero Madau, Evan Schneider
Year: 2022
Abstract: The forest of Lyman-$α$ absorption lines detected in the spectra of distant quasars encodes information on the nature and properties of dark matter and the thermodynamics of diffuse baryonic material. Its main observable -- the 1D flux power spectrum (FPS) -- should exhibit a suppression on small scales and an enhancement on large scales in warm dark matter (WDM) cosmologies compared to standard $Λ$CDM. Here, we present an unprecedented suite of 1080 high-resolution cosmological hydrodynamical simulations run with the Graphics Processing Unit-accelerated code Cholla to study the evolution of the Lyman-$α$ forest under a wide range of physically-motivated gas thermal histories along with different free-streaming lengths of WDM thermal relics in the early Universe. A statistical comparison of synthetic data with the forest FPS measured down to the smallest velocity scales ever probed at redshifts $4.0\lesssim z\lesssim 5.2$ (Boera et al. 2019) yields a lower limit $m_{\rm WDM}>3.1$ keV (95 percent CL) for the WDM particle mass and constrains the amplitude and spectrum of the photoheating and photoionizing background produced by star-forming galaxies and active galactic nuclei at these redshifts. Interestingly, our Bayesian inference analysis appears to weakly favor WDM models with a peak likelihood value at the thermal relic mass of $m_{\rm WDM}=4.5$ keV. We find that the suppression of the FPS from free-streaming saturates at $k\gtrsim 0.1\,\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{km}^{-1}$ because of peculiar velocity smearing, and this saturated suppression combined with a slightly lower gas temperature provides a moderately better fit to the observed small-scale FPS for WDM cosmologies.

---

# keV sterile-neutrino dark matter recipe

A keV sterile neutrino decays radiatively nu_s -> nu + gamma, giving an
X-ray line at E = m_s / 2 with rate Gamma = 1.36e-32 s^-1 (sin^2 2theta /
1e-10)(m_s / keV)^5. This recipe checks a candidate against X-ray,
abundance and structure-formation constraints.

## 1. One candidate, all targets — one call

`predict_sterile_nu_xray_line(m_s_eV=..., sin2_2theta=..., target="all")`
returns the line energy, lifetime, the whole-halo flux for every target
ranked by brightness, and which tabulated limits exclude it. Do not loop
over targets.

## 2. Is it the dark matter?

`predict_sterile_nu` (or `predict_sterile_nu_grid` for several candidates)
gives Omega_s h^2 (DW, or SF with a lepton asymmetry), `overcloses`
(Omega_s h^2 > 0.12), Delta N_eff (tiny for keV DM — BBN does not constrain
it), and the free-streaming length. For DW production, the mixing needed
for the full relic density at m_s ~ 7 keV is already X-ray excluded — say
so; resonant (SF) production is the surviving option.

## 3. The plane

`scan_sterile_nu_parameters(m_min_eV=1e3, m_max_eV=1e5, theta_min=1e-14,
theta_max=1e-6)` then `plot_sterile_nu_exclusion(scan_file=<its NPZ>)`:
overclosure region, Omega_DM line, NuSTAR/XMM limits, Lyman-alpha bound,
3.5 keV point.

## Caveats you must state

- **Fluxes are whole-halo** with the sterile neutrino as all of the dark
  matter: no field-of-view cut, no density-profile integration. Compare to
  a measured line flux only as an order-of-magnitude check.
- **X-ray limits are tabulated points** (NuSTAR M31, XMM blank sky);
  "excluded_by" checks limits within 30% in mass only.
- **Lyman-alpha**: 5.3 keV is the THERMAL-relic WDM bound; the equivalent
  bound on a DW sterile neutrino mass is several times higher.
- **The 3.5 keV line is debated** (Dessert+ 2020 blank-sky exclusion).
"
  }
}

tool_calls.result:
arXiv ID: 1702.08430
Title: keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter
Authors: Alexander Merle
Year: 2017
Abstract: We give an overview of the current status of keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter. After a short introduction, we start by a general discussion of non-thermal production of Dark Matter, which applies to the three most commonly discussed mechanisms to produce sterile neutrino Dark Matter in the Universe: non-resonant, resonant, and decay production. The main goal in each case is to compute the momentum distribution function $f(p,t)$, which incorporates the full information about the Dark Matter setting under consideration, at least in what concerns its cosmological aspects. While some difficulties lie in the actual computation of this quantity, it is decisive to obtain bounds from cosmic structure formation, which turn out to be the most crucial ones to distinguish different types of production. We will introduce these bounds and we put the resulting limits into a proper context, thereby illustrating that a significant amount of relevant parameter space is available, part of which is testable in particular by Lyman-$α$ data.

args.claim: The sterile-nu server gives DW Omega_s h^2 proportional to sin^2 2theta. At sin^2 2theta = 1e-12 it returns Omega_s h^2 = 0.003041 (20 keV), 0.00361 (22 keV), 0.005936 (29 keV), 0.01309 (45 keV) and 0.0004715 (7.1 keV). Linear scaling to f_s = Omega_s h^2/0.12 = 1 then gives sin^2 2theta(f_s=1) of about 3.95e-11, 3.32e-11, 2.02e-11, 9.17e-12 and 2.55e-10 respectively. At the 3.5 keV line point (7.1 keV, 7e-11) the tool gives Omega_s h^2 = 0.033, i.e. f_s = 0.275.
args.note: Linearity was checked in the 374-point grid: at 3 keV, Omega h^2 = 1e-4 at 1e-12 and 1e-3 at 1e-11. The f_s = 1 mixings come from linear rescaling by me, not directly from the tool. Omega_dm h^2 = 0.120 is the tool's reference value.

args.claim: At the DW f_s = 1 mixing, the tool's X-ray check gives: 20 keV with sin^2 2theta = 3.95e-11 is EXCLUDED by NuSTAR M31 (Roach+ 2020); 29 keV (2.02e-11) and 45 keV (9.17e-12) are 'not excluded', but only because no tabulated limit lies within 30% in mass. Those two masses are uncovered by the tool, not shown to be allowed. The tool also does not return the numerical limit on sin^2 2theta, so f_s at the X-ray limit cannot be read directly from it.
args.note: The skill states that X-ray limits are tabulated points (NuSTAR M31, XMM blank sky) and that excluded_by checks limits within 30% in mass only. The d-04 literature limits are needed to fill the 29-45 keV range.

arXiv ID: 2209.14220
Title: New Constraints on Warm Dark Matter from the Lyman-$α$ Forest Power Spectrum
Authors: Bruno Villasenor, Brant Robertson, Piero Madau, Evan Schneider
Year: 2022
Abstract: The forest of Lyman-$α$ absorption lines detected in the spectra of distant quasars encodes information on the nature and properties of dark matter and the thermodynamics of diffuse baryonic material. Its main observable -- the 1D flux power spectrum (FPS) -- should exhibit a suppression on small scales and an enhancement on large scales in warm dark matter (WDM) cosmologies compared to standard $Λ$CDM. Here, we present an unprecedented suite of 1080 high-resolution cosmological hydrodynamical simulations run with the Graphics Processing Unit-accelerated code Cholla to study the evolution of the Lyman-$α$ forest under a wide range of physically-motivated gas thermal histories along with different free-streaming lengths of WDM thermal relics in the early Universe. A statistical comparison of synthetic data with the forest FPS measured down to the smallest velocity scales ever probed at redshifts $4.0\lesssim z\lesssim 5.2$ (Boera et al. 2019) yields a lower limit $m_{\rm WDM}>3.1$ keV (95 percent CL) for the WDM particle mass and constrains the amplitude and spectrum of the photoheating and photoionizing background produced by star-forming galaxies and active galactic nuclei at these redshifts. Interestingly, our Bayesian inference analysis appears to weakly favor WDM models with a peak likelihood value at the thermal relic mass of $m_{\rm WDM}=4.5$ keV. We find that the suppression of the FPS from free-streaming saturates at $k\gtrsim 0.1\,\mathrm{s}\,\mathrm{km}^{-1}$ because of peculiar velocity smearing, and this saturated suppression combined with a slightly lower gas temperature provides a moderately better fit to the observed small-scale FPS for WDM cosmologies.

arXiv ID: 1306.2314
Title: Warm Dark Matter as a solution to the small scale crisis: new constraints from high redshift Lyman-alpha forest data
Authors: M. Viel, G. D. Becker, J. S. Bolton, M. G. Haehnelt
Year: 2013
Abstract: We present updated constraints on the free-streaming of warm dark matter (WDM) particles derived from an analysis of the Lya flux power spectrum measured from high-resolution spectra of 25 z > 4 quasars obtained with the Keck High Resolution Echelle Spectrometer (HIRES) and the Magellan Inamori Kyocera Echelle (MIKE) spectrograph. We utilize a new suite of high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations that explore WDM masses of 1, 2 and 4 keV (assuming the WDM consists of thermal relics), along with different physically motivated thermal histories. We carefully address different sources of systematic error that may affect our final results and perform an analysis of the Lya flux power with conservative error estimates. By using a method that samples the multi-dimensional astrophysical and cosmological parameter space, we obtain a lower limit mwdm > 3.3 keV (2sigma) for warm dark matter particles in the form of early decoupled thermal relics. Adding the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Lya flux power spectrum does not improve this limit. Thermal relics of masses 1 keV, 2 keV and 2.5 keV are disfavoured by the data at about the 9sigma, 4sigma and 3sigma C.L., respectively. Our analysis disfavours WDM models where there is a suppression in the linear matter power spectrum at (non-linear) scales corresponding to k=10h/Mpc which deviates more than 10% from a LCDM model. Given this limit, the corresponding "free-streaming mass" below which the mass function may be suppressed is 2x10^8 Msun/h. There is thus very little room for a contribution of the free-streaming of WDM to the solution of what has been termed the small scale crisis of cold dark matter.

arXiv ID: 1702.01764
Title: New Constraints on the free-streaming of warm dark matter from intermediate and small scale Lyman-$α$ forest data
Authors: Vid Iršič, Matteo Viel, Martin G. Haehnelt, James S. Bolton, Stefano Cristiani, George D. Becker, Valentina D'Odorico, Guido Cupani, Tae-Sun Kim, Trystyn A. M. Berg, Sebastian López, Sara Ellison, Lise Christensen, Kelly D. Denny, Gábor Worseck
Year: 2017
Abstract: We present new measurements of the free-streaming of warm dark matter (WDM) from Lyman-$α$ flux-power spectra. We use data from the medium resolution, intermediate redshift XQ-100 sample observed with the X-shooter spectrograph ($z=3 - 4.2$) and the high-resolution, high-redshift sample used in Viel et al. (2013) obtained with the HIRES/MIKE spectrographs ($z=4.2 - 5.4$). Based on further improved modelling of the dependence of the Lyman-$α$ flux-power spectrum on the free-streaming of dark matter, cosmological parameters, as well as the thermal history of the intergalactic medium (IGM) with hydrodynamical simulations, we obtain the following limits, expressed as the equivalent mass of thermal relic WDM particles. The XQ-100 flux power spectrum alone gives a lower limit of 1.4 keV, the re-analysis of the HIRES/MIKE sample gives 4.1 keV while the combined analysis gives our best and significantly strengthened lower limit of 5.3 keV (all 2$σ$ C.L.). The further improvement in the joint analysis is partly due to the fact that the two data sets have different degeneracies between astrophysical and cosmological parameters that are broken when the data sets are combined, and more importantly on chosen priors on the thermal evolution. These results all assume that the temperature evolution of the IGM can be modelled as a power law in redshift. Allowing for a non-smooth evolution of the temperature of the IGM with sudden temperature changes of up to 5000K reduces the lower limit for the combined analysis to 3.5 keV. A WDM with smaller thermal relic masses would require, however, a sudden temperature jump of $5000\,K$ or more in the narrow redshift interval $z=4.6-4.8$, in disagreement with observations of the thermal history based on high-resolution resolution Lyman-$α$ forest data and expectations for photo-heating and cooling in the low density IGM at these redshifts.

We give an overview of the current status of keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter. After a short
introduction, we start by a general discussion of non-thermal production of Dark Matter, which
applies to the three most commonly discussed mechanisms to produce sterile neutrino Dark Mat-
ter in the Universe: non-resonant, resonant, and decay production. The main goal in each case is
to compute the momentum distribution function f (p,t), which incorporates the full information
about the Dark Matter setting under consideration, at least in what concerns its cosmological as-
pects. While some difﬁculties lie in the actual computation of this quantity, it is decisive to obtain
bounds from cosmic structure formation, which turn out to be the most crucial ones to distinguish
different types of production. We will introduce these bounds and we put the resulting limits
into a proper context, thereby illustrating that a signiﬁcant amount of relevant parameter space is
available, part of which is testable in particular by Lyman-α data.

3. Production of keV sterile neutrinos by active-sterile mixing
The most natural approach is to produce sterile neutrinos by their admixture to the active-
neutrino sector [ 4, 5, 6, 7], which exploits the fact that any reaction producing active neutrinos
can also produce steriles – only with a much smaller probability – as long as some active-sterile
mixing angles are non-zero. This could gradually produce enough sterile neutrinos to explain the
observed amount of DM, but the resulting spectrum would feature too many particles with rather
large momenta, making this setting similar to a hot DM case and thus excluded by data.
However, this could change for the case of a lepton number asymmetry being present in the
early Universe, a suitable value of which can resonantly enhance the transitions from active to
sterile neutrinos [6, 8, 9, 10]. While the origin of such an asymmetry has to be explained at ﬁrst,
its effects have been computed. Basically, if the asymmetry is large enough, it produces very
many sterile neutrinos at a very speciﬁc combination of momentum and temperature. Thus, in the
momentum distribution function, a sharp peak appears on top of a continuous spectrum, clearly
comprising a non-thermal distribution. If this peak is located at a comparatively small momentum,
i.e., a big fraction of the sterile neutrinos are not very fast, the resulting spectrum should be “cooler”
(i.e., smaller momenta are more dominant) than the one resulting from non-resonant production.
It is non-trivial to obtain statements from cosmic structure formation about non-thermal spec-
tra, cf. left Fig. 1, so that new methods have to be developed to do so. Confronting resonant
production with data, it turns out that the “coldest” region, which would be closest to the cold DM
case, is located in a region of the parameter space that is by far excluded from the X-ray bound (i.e.,
from not observing the photons stemming from sterile neutrino DM decay,N→ νγ ). All parameter
combinations that are left can be investigated to see whether they are compatible with cosmic struc-
ture formation. This has been done in Ref. [15], using a modiﬁed version of the so-called extended
Press-Schechter approach. Two methods have been applied to the spectra resulting from resonant
production: halo counting (i.e., whether a given DM distribution produces at least as many small
haloes as dwarf galaxies are observed) and the Lyman-α method (i.e., whether the distribution of
the intergalactic medium coincides with the DM distribution expected from the spectrum under
consideration). The result was that, contrary to some statements in the literature which did not take
into account bounds from structure formation, resonant production is pushed already by current
data. Thus, depending on how aggressively the Lyman- α data is interpreted, resonant production
may even be completely excluded. However, it is in any case correct to say that structure formation
does yield a strong constraint on this production mechanism, cf. Fig. 2.
4. Production of keV sterile neutrinos by particle decays
Production by particle decays is an alternative way to generate keV sterile neutrino DM, by
ﬁrst producing a parent particle (e.g., a singlet scalar S) which then decays into sterile neutrinos
(e.g., S→ NN). Typically, the decisive parameters are the Higgs portal coupling λ, which drives
the production of the scalar from Standard Model particles, and the Yukawa coupling y, which
drives the decay. Depending on whether the scalar itself equilibrates [ 11] or not [ 12], different
(non-thermal) spectra are possible, some resembling e.g. the green curve plotted in the left Fig. 1.

constraints on the mass of light gravitinos with realistic

a pure ΛWDM model. In Section IVB, we will obtain an
upper limit for the mass of light gravitinos in a mixed
ΛCWDM universe. Section V contains our conclusions
and some comments on the implications of our results

eﬃcient way.
In this work, we present a framework for cosmologi-
cal dark matter bounds, speciﬁcally using the Lyman-
alpha forest, which makes the testing of new models ro-
bust, accurate and computationally eﬃcient. This com-
bines a general model for the eﬀect of non-cold dark mat-
ter (nCDM) on the matter power spectrum presented in
Ref. [36] with the Bayesian emulator optimization we pre-

training data in order to determine the peak of the pos-

cosmological bounds from the Lyman-alpha forest [e. g.,

cial point. Ref. [30] interpolate using “ordinary kriging”,
which has some similarity to the method we consider
here, although they do not model full parameter covari-
ance nor test for convergence using Bayesian optimization
(see § III B). The emulator model we use makes fewer as-
sumptions and is more robust in its statistical modeling,
which can remove bias in power spectrum estimation and
strengthen parameter constraints [42]. Even for cosmo-
logical datasets where emulators are already used, the
combination of convergence tests using Bayesian opti-
mization and eﬀective theories as described above can
provide signiﬁcant beneﬁts.
In § II, we present the general emulator for nCDM
models and then in § III, we present the example of op-
timizing the emulator for the study of ULA dark mat-

validation in § IV, discuss in § V and conclude in § VI.

II. NON-COLD DARK MATTER EMULATOR
In this section, we present a general emulator of hydro-
dynamical simulations for non-cold dark matter models
using the Lyman-alpha forest ﬂux power spectrum as the
constraining data. This initial emulator is not tied to a
speciﬁc dark matter model, but rather forms the base for
Bayesian optimization for a particular model (see§ III for
the example of ultra-light axions). This framework en-
sures the computational eﬃciency, theoretical accuracy
and maximum precision for dark matter bounds using
the cosmic large-scale structure. In § II A, we explain
the non-cold dark matter model we employ, ﬁrst intro-
duced by Ref. [36]. We present the details of our cos-
mological hydrodynamical simulations in § II B and the
intergalactic medium and background cosmology model
which must be marginalized in § II C. In § II D, we dis-
cuss the method of emulation by Gaussian processes and
how this connects to Bayesian inference.

which is as general and powerful as possible, we employ
the non-cold dark matter (nCDM) model ﬁrst introduced
by Ref. [36]. The model is deﬁned by a “transfer func-
tion”,

C. Intergalactic medium and cosmological model
In order to study nCDM models using the ﬂux power
spectrum, we must marginalize over uncertainty in the
thermal and ionization history of the IGM (which partly
derives from the uncertain nature of cosmic reionization),
as well as relevant aspects of the cosmological model.
1. Pressure smoothing
The energy deposited in the IGM by the background
of ionizing ultra-violet (UV) photons and the ﬁnite tem-
perature of the IGM (∼ 104 K at z∼ 5) leads to a few
diﬀerent observable eﬀects in the ﬂux power spectrum.
The heat in the IGM smoothes the spatial distribution
of the gas below a characteristic scale, where the gas pres-
sure balances gravitational clustering. A simple, classical
interpretation deﬁnes a Jeans pressure smoothing scale,
which is a function of the instantaneous gas temperature
[e. g., 66]. However, in an expanding universe with an
evolving thermal state, the relevant pressure smoothing
scale depends on the integrated history of the gas heating
as spatial ﬂuctuations from earlier times expand or fail
to collapse depending on the temperature at that epoch.
This “ﬁltering length” in general deviates from the Jeans
length, being typically greater before reionization and
less afterwards (∼ 100 comoving kpc at z∼ 5).
In order to track the heat deposited in our simulations
and the resulting ﬁltering scale, we use the integrated
energy deposited into the gas per unit mass at the mean
density,

third is the “angular-momentum” problem of CDM halos,

galaxies, which can be alleviated by the hindrance of gas
collapse and angular momentum loss through the delay of
small halo formation in a WDM scenario [23]. The fourth
problem is the formation of disk-dominated or pure-disk
galaxies in CDM models, which is impeded by bulge for-
mation due to the high merger accretion rate history in
CDM models, but may be alleviated with WDM [24, 25].

and dark matter can arise in grand uniﬁed models [26],
string-inspired models [27], and models with large ex-
tra dimensions [28, 29]. In reverence to Occam’s ra-
zor, the minimalist model of Ref. [30] produces the

and the resulting global asymmetry in the ejecta alone
can power the observed distribution of pulsar velocities
remains an open question [36, 37].
The potentially beneﬁcial eﬀects of the suppression
of cosmological small-scale structure in WDM can also
lead to observational conﬂicts if the suppression extends
to excessively high mass and length scales. As I shall
show in detail below, the suppression scale monotoni-
cally decreases with increasing sterile neutrino particle
mass. The reionization of the universe by a redshift of
z ∼ 6 requires suﬃcient structure formation at very early
times, and can place one of the most stringent lower-
bounds on the sterile neutrino mass [38, 39]. The ra-
diative decay of the sterile neutrino dark matter may,
however, increase the hydrogen ionization fraction, aug-
menting molecular hydrogen formation, gas cooling, star
formation, and therefore reionization [40]. One of the
best direct measures of clustering at small scales is the
clustering observed in intervening gas along the line-of-
sight to a quasar, known as the Lyman- α forest [41].
Statistically-consistent constraints allowing freedom in
all cosmological parameters and constraints from the cos-
mic microwave background, galaxy clustering, and a mea-
surement of clustering in the Lyman- α forest gives a lower
limit for the sterile neutrino dark matter particle mass as
ms > 1.7 keV (95% CL) [42].

any variance in the ﬂux of both components, and we ﬁnd
that the best-ﬁt GRXE ﬂux is consistent with Galactic

ally, we ﬁnd that allowing both the CXB and GRXE
ﬂuxes to vary leads to best-ﬁt values which are inconsis-
tent with the previously-described measurements of these
components’ ﬂux levels.
We parameterize our DM line signal in xspec with a
vanishingly-narrow Gaussian—i.e., a δ-function in E—
as the intrinsic width of any DM line is expected to be
much less than the ∼0.4 keV detector energy resolution
with which it is convolved. Our treatment of the DM line
during the line-search procedure is described further in
Sec. III A.
The ﬂuxes of the astrophysical components in our spec-
tral model—CXB, GRXE, and DM line—are attenuated
by absorption and scattering in the interstellar medium
(ISM). This attenuation is parameterized in terms of
the equivalent column density of neutral hydrogen, NH,
via the tbabs model in xspec [118]. We adopt ﬁxed
values of 7 .0× 1020 cm−2 for obsID 40410001002 and
1.1× 1021 cm−2 for obsID 40410002002 [119, 120]. (Both
FPMs share the same NH value, which is assumed to
be constant across the 0-bounce and 2-bounce FOVs de-
spite the somewhat diﬀerent sky coverage and values of
∆Ω0b from A/B.) This corresponds to an optical depth
τ ≲ 10−2 at E = 5 keV, falling steeply with increasing
energy. Although the ﬂux attenuation from the ISM is a
≲ 1% eﬀect across the energy range of this analysis, we
include it for consistency.
Finally, we consider the absorption of x-rays within
the NuSTAR instrument itself. Before incoming astro-
physical x-rays (from the CXB, GRXE, or DM) strike
the detectors, they must pass through a ∼100-µm beryl-
lium shield with transmission eﬃciency EBe(E), rising
from ∼0.67 at E = 3 keV to ∼0.92 at E = 5 keV.
(The treatment of EBe is discussed further in Sec. II C.)
An additional absorption eﬀect arises in the detectors
themselves. The CdZnTe detectors have a ∼0.11-µm
Pt contact coating, as well as a ∼0.27-µm layer of inac-
tive CdZnTe (both varying somewhat between individual
detector crystals), through which incoming x-rays must
pass [99]. At E = 5 keV, these detector components re-
sult in a ﬂux attenuation of∼25%, though this decreases
quickly with increasing energy [32]. These detector ab-
sorption eﬀects (often called nuabs or detabs) are in-
cluded in every spectral component except the internal
continuum.
As shown in Figs. 3 and 4, the model described in
Sec. II D provides an acceptable ﬁt to the NuSTAR spec-
tra across most of the 5–20 keV energy range (see Figs. 3
and 4 for the reduced-χ2 and corresponding p-values for
each spectrum), but there are several deviations from
the model that may aﬀect our derived line ﬂux lim-
its, and thus require further consideration. The higher
χ2 in FPMA of obsID 40410001002A is due to the en-
ergy range 15–20 keV (excluding this energy range yields
χ2/47 = 0.94 with p = 0.59), and similarly for FPMB of
obsID 40410002002B in the energy range 8–9 keV (yield-
ing χ2/54 = 1 .15 with p = 0.21). As both of these
regions are excesses with respect to the default back-
ground model, the DM line ﬂux limits in the mass ranges
mχ≃ 16 keV and 30–40 keV are correspondingly weak-
ened (see Sec. III B), as we use a conservative line-search
procedure in which the DM line ﬂux is allowed to ﬁll the
excess (see Sec. III A). In Sec. III B, we perform Monte
Carlo simulations to verify that our constraint is con-
sistent with one limited by statistical variations in our
measurement, not systematic variations due to incom-
plete modeling.

discuss the implications for sterile-neutrino dark matter
(Sec. III C).

B. Sensitivity Estimation with Simulations
To validate our results, we perform line searches in
mock spectra to ﬁnd the expected upper limits when the
spectra are purely statistically limited. This exercise also
allows us to further study the deviations discussed in
Sec. II D.
Instead of fully mimicking the actual analysis, where
we analyze each module separately and then combine the
constraints, we simplify the procedure by considering a
single spectrum (rather than all four) per mock analysis
to speed up the computation. We generate 100 Monte
Carlo (MC) spectra with no DM line, using the fakeit
tool in xspec. Each spectrum has 200 ks exposure, and
is generated using the best-ﬁt spectral model of FPMA,
obsID 40410001002. This simpliﬁcation is motivated by
the fact that the spectrum for each module has similar
best-ﬁt model parameters, and hence statistics. We also
test the results obtained with 10 of these simpliﬁed sim-
ulations against 10 full realizations (i.e., including both
obsIDs and both FPMs) and ﬁnd good agreement. We
then pass these mock spectra through the same ﬁtting
and line-search procedure as the data. At each mass bin,
we thus have 100 simulated upper limits. We interpo-
late the cumulative distribution of these upper limits and
ﬁnd the corresponding 68% and 95% intervals. The up-
per limits can then obtained directly from the line-search
procedure (see Sec. III A) without needing to combine
diﬀerent FPMs.

V. DISCUSSION
A. Dark matter model
The model we employ to describe the eﬀect of non-cold
dark matter on the matter power spectrum [ﬁrst intro-
duced in 36] can characterize many diﬀerent dark mat-
ter candidates with diﬀerent physical mechanisms sup-
pressing the small-scale power spectrum. These include,
e. g., warm dark matter with a free streaming scale [e. g.,
101] or dark matter interacting with itself or baryons
[e. g., 20, 25]; this is discussed further in Ref. [36]. For
the nCDM model to apply, the detectable eﬀect on the
power spectrum relative to the cold dark matter limit
must be fully captured by modiﬁed initial conditions
at z ∼ 100. We consider here and in an accompany-
ing data analysis [83], the example of ultra-light axion
dark matter ( § III). We ﬁt the nCDM model to ULA
matter power spectra calculated by the modiﬁed Boltz-
mann code axionCAMB [86, see § III A]. We ﬁnd the ﬁt
to be good aside from suppressed small-scale power spec-
trum oscillations which cannot be captured by the nCDM
model. We argue, however, that given the precision of
ﬂux power spectrum measurements on the relevant scales
[∼ 10% to 25%; 64], these suppressed oscillations are cur-
rently undetectable and so the nCDM model captures the
relevant phenomenology. This compares to the approx-
imate ULA power spectrum transfer function employed
in previous Lyman-

7.3. Summary
We have shown in this section that if the lower bound on Ms from the Lyman- α data is
indeed as found in refs. [32, 33], then there is no parameter s pace left within the νMSM to
realize the scenario of sterile neutrinos serving as warm da rk matter, respecting the “crucial”
assumptions (i)–(iii) of Sec. 1.
Of course, this does not mean that the sterile neutrino is exc luded as a dark matter candi-
date, but that at least one of the assumptions would have to be relaxed for this to be the case.
For instance, sterile neutrinos could be produced mainly in interactions beyond the νMSM, as
in ref. [5]. Another logical possibility is that the Univers e had substantial leptonic asymme-
tries at small temperatures, leading to a resonant producti on of sterile neutrinos [8]. In any
event, for Ms > 3. 5 keV (6 keV if all hadronic uncertainties are pushed in one di rection and
the strongest X-ray bounds are relaxed by a factor of two) the active-sterile transitions from
the thermal charge-symmetric plasma cannot produce cosmol ogically interesting amounts of
sterile neutrino dark matter.

8. Conclusions
In this paper we have studied the production of sterile neutr inos in the νMSM through active-
sterile neutrino transitions from a thermal plasma, which d oes not contain any signiﬁcant
asymmetries related to lepton numbers. Though a ﬁrst-princ iples formula for the production
rate exists, which is valid to all orders in the strong coupli ng constant, its practical evaluation
is subject to a number of uncertainties related to the strong interactions. The purpose of this
