paper has been to present a realistic “mean” evaluation of th e hadronic contributions, and
to estimate conservatively all the uncertainties that this mean result is subject to.
The most important result of this paper is encoded in the four lines shown in Fig. 9. They
correspond to the case when there is no entropy production ( S = 1) due to the decay of the
heavier sterile neutrinos of the νMSM. The area above the dotted line is certainly excluded:
the amount of dark matter produced would lead to the overclos ure of the Universe. The region
below the dashed line is certainly allowed: the amount of ste rile neutrinos produced due to
active-sterile transitions is smaller than the amount of da rk matter observed. Any point in
the region between the two solid lines (corresponding to the “most reasonable” model for
the hadronic contributions that we have been able to come up w ith) can lead to dark matter
generation entirely due to active-sterile transitions. A m aximal variation of the parameters
of our hadronic model extends this region to the space betwee n the dotted and dashed lines.
In the case of entropy production with a factor S > 1. 0, all these four lines simply move up
by a factor S.

args.claim: Roach et al. 2022 (arXiv:2207.04572, NuSTAR Milky Way halo, about 7 Ms/detector blank-sky plus about 20 Ms/detector stacked data) find no anomalous lines and set sin^2(2theta) limits for m_s = 6-40 keV. Quote: "we strongly disfavor a ~7-keV sterile neutrino decaying into a 3.5-keV photon" and "we derive leading limits on sterile neutrinos with masses ~15–18 keV and ~25–40 keV, reaching or extending below the big bang nucleosynthesis limit". The conclusions add that the parameter space "is now mostly covered", but this "does not fully rule out sterile neutrinos as the only DM component"; it shows "the simple and elegant mixing production mechanism [8, 9] may be insufficient". The authors therefore do NOT claim that X-ray data alone exclude 100% DW dark matter. Their "mostly covered" statement relies on adding satellite-counting bounds.

args.claim: Roach et al. 2020 (arXiv:1908.09037, NuSTAR Galactic bulge, about 190 ks) give 95% one-sided limits on the decay rate Gamma for m_s = 10-40 keV, quoted in Gamma [s^-1] rather than sin^2 2theta. Their Fig. 5 plots these limits on a Gamma axis spanning 1e-29 to 1e-27 s^-1, compared with Neronov+2016, Perez+2017 and Ng+2019. The paper states the limits are "comparable to previous NuSTAR limits" and improve on earlier ones by about 2x at 10-12 keV. They are weakened near m ~ 16 keV and 30-40 keV, where the background fit shows excesses. No numerical values were tabulated, and the curves were not digitised.

args.claim: Viel et al. 2005 (astro-ph/0501562) Eq. (5), checked against the full text: m_sterile = 4.43 keV (m_thermal/1 keV)^{4/3} (0.25(0.7)^2/omega_x)^{1/3}. The coefficient 4.43 keV and the exponents 4/3 and -1/3 are confirmed, and 0.25*0.49 = 0.1225 matches the board's normalisation. The paper derives it by 'equating omega_x and m_x/T_x' of a thermal relic and a sterile neutrino 'which share the same phase-space distribution but with an overall suppression factor chi'. So it treats the DW spectrum as a rescaled Fermi-Dirac distribution with T_x = T_nu, and the two transfer functions are identical by construction.
args.note: Quote on page 3 of the extracted text, Eq. (5). Not yet added to references.bib with cite().

args.claim: The Viel 2005 transfer-function fit, checked against the full text, is T(k) = [1+(alpha k)^{2nu}]^{-5/nu} with nu = 1.12 (best fit for k < 5 h/Mpc). For thermal relics alpha = 0.049 (m_x/1 keV)^{-1.11} (Omega_x/0.25)^{0.11} (h/0.7)^{1.22} h^-1 Mpc; the general form is alpha = 0.24 ((m_x/T_x)/(1 keV/T_nu))^{-0.83} (omega_x/0.1225)^{-0.16} Mpc. The half-mode condition T^2 = 1/2 gives k_hm = (2^{nu/10}-1)^{1/(2nu)}/alpha = 0.325/alpha (my own arithmetic). Taking Omega_x = 0.25 and h = 0.7, the thermal limits give alpha = 0.01396, 0.01302, 0.01024 and 0.00710 h^-1 Mpc, so k_hm is about 23.3, 25.0, 31.8 and 45.8 h/Mpc for 3.1, 3.3, 4.1 and 5.7 keV. Under Viel's mapping the DW k_hm at the mapped mass is identical by construction.
args.note: alpha and k_hm values are hand arithmetic on the quoted Eq. (7), not tool outputs. The fit was calibrated only for k < 5 h/Mpc, so k_hm of about 23-46 h/Mpc is an extrapolation.

args.claim: The general nCDM framework of 2007.13751 (Murgia et al. form) uses T(k) = [1+(alpha k)^beta]^gamma at z = 99, which reduces to the thermal WDM fit when beta = 2nu, gamma = -5/nu and nu = 1.12. A 2 keV WDM is fitted by [alpha, beta, gamma] = [0.02, 2.2, -4.5], with priors alpha in [0, 0.1], beta in [1, 10] and gamma in [-10, 0]. In the sections read, the paper gives no DW-specific relation between thermal-relic and sterile mass; it is applied to ultra-light axions. Using it for DW would require fitting (alpha, beta, gamma) to a Boltzmann-code DW transfer function.

args.claim: The sterile-nu server's DW yield gives a smaller f_s=1 mixing than both published fits I read: sin^2 2theta(f_s=1) is 2.55e-10, 3.95e-11, 3.32e-11, 2.02e-11 and 9.17e-12 at 7.1, 20, 22, 29 and 45 keV (from the CSV rows at sin^2 2theta = 1e-12: Omega_s h^2 = 0.000471462, 0.00304114, 0.00361029, 0.00593606, 0.0130907). The Abazajian 2006 fit gives 3.02e-10 x10 = 3.02e-9, 5.61e-10, 4.80e-10, 3.06e-10 and 1.50e-10, which is 11.9, 14.2, 14.4, 15.2 and 16.4 times the tool's values. The Asaka-Laine-Shaposhnikov 'most conservative' upper-bound line gives 7.88e-10, 1.30e-10, 1.10e-10, 6.79e-11 and 3.16e-11, which is 3.10, 3.29, 3.31, 3.36 and 3.44 times the tool's values. So the tool produces 3 to 16 times more DW dark matter per unit mixing than these fits.
args.note: Abazajian 2006 Eq. 7, verbatim from the full text: 'ms = 3.40 keV (sin2 2θ/10−8)^−0.615 (ΩDM/0.26)^0.5 × {0.527 erfc[...]}'. The braces equal 1 at TQCD = 170 MeV, and the fit is for electron flavour. Inverted, this gives s = 1e-8 (m/3.40 keV)^(-1/0.615). I took Omega_DM = 0.26, which is about 0.12/h^2 for h = 0.68. ALS (hep-ph/0612182, Sec. 7.1), verbatim: 'the most conservative bound from Eq. (7.1) becomes log10[sin22θ] <∼ −7.6195−1.7428 log10[Ms/keV]+log10[S]', with S = 1. This fit is stated for Ms <= 4 keV, so using it at 7-45 keV is an extrapolation. It is the overclosure upper line (maximal hadronic uncertainty), so ALS's own 'mean' f_s=1 line lies below it and the factor of ~3 is a lower limit. All arithmetic is mine. cite() was not run, because the budget ran out, so the quotes were read in the full text but not validated through cite(). The mass dependence also differs: the tool scales as Omega proportional to m^1.80 at fixed mixing (20 to 45 keV), while Abazajian's fit gives m^2 s^1.23.
